title: How would you replace a legacy service without a big-bang migration: find a boundary where traffic or responsibility can move incrementally (a strangler-fig pattern, a compatibility layer, shadow traffic, parallel validation, or consumer-by-consumer cutover): and why must the design include how the organization RETURNS to the previous state when the new path misbehaves?
shortTitle: How would you replace a legacy service without a big-bang migration?
keyPoints: A big-bang rewrite concentrates all risk into one switch-over moment with no gradual learning and often no safe way back.
The strangler-fig pattern places a routing facade in front of the legacy service and moves one slice at a time.
Shadow traffic sends real requests to both services, returns the legacy response, and compares the new response without customer impact.
Parallel validation flags any behavioral divergence before the new service is ever authoritative.
Cut over by percentage (1%, 10%, 50%, 100%) with a compatibility layer so callers do not change in lockstep.
Every increment must include a designed, fast, rehearsed return path to legacy (feature flag or routing rule).
The legacy must remain functional with current data during migration so flipping back never loses data.

s1_definition.oneliner: Put a router in front of the legacy service and move one capability or slice at a time to the new one -- validating in parallel and keeping an instant path back -- until the legacy is strangled and retired.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Strangler-Fig Pattern** – a facade routes traffic; initially all goes to legacy, then progressively more goes to the new service until legacy handles nothing and can be retired.
- **Shadow Traffic** – the facade sends real requests to both, returns the legacy response, and discards the new one after comparing.
- **Parallel Validation** – compares responses from both services and flags divergence before the new service is authoritative.
- **Compatibility Layer** – translates between old and new contracts so callers do not change in lockstep.
- **Percentage Ramp** – cut over by percentage (1%, 10%, 50%, 100%) watching metrics at each step.
- **Return Path** – a designed, fast, rehearsed way back to legacy for every increment (feature flag, routing rule).
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants to replace its decades-old transaction system but cannot switch everything overnight. So they put a receptionist (router) in front. At first every request goes to the old system. Then they quietly send just balance enquiries to the new system while everything else stays on the old one, double-checking answers. If it works, they move deposits, then transfers, one capability at a time, keeping the old system ready to take over instantly if the new one gives a wrong answer.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Strangler-Fig Migration
  ───────────────────────

  Phase 1: Shadow
  Client ──► Facade ──► Legacy (response returned)
                   └──► New (response compared, discarded)

  Phase 2: Ramp by percentage
  Client ──► Facade ──► Legacy (90%)
                   └──► New (10%, observed)

  Phase 3: Full cutover
  Client ──► Facade ──► New (100%)
                        Legacy (standby, ready for rollback)

  Phase 4: Retire
  Client ──► Facade ──► New (100%)
                        Legacy decommissioned

  At EVERY phase: flip feature flag → instant rollback to Legacy
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Never replace a legacy service with a big-bang rewrite. The strangler-fig pattern spreads the risk across many small, reversible steps. A routing facade sits in front of legacy, and you move one slice at a time: shadow traffic first to compare, then percentage ramp to build confidence, then full cutover.

Before trusting the new service, de-risk with shadow traffic and parallel validation. Send real requests to both, return the legacy response, and flag any divergence. Only when divergence is zero do you cut over, usually ramping by percentage with a compatibility layer so callers do not change in lockstep.

Every increment must include a designed, fast, rehearsed return path. A feature flag or routing rule must be flippable instantly, and the legacy must remain functional with current data so flipping back never loses data. Test the rollback before the cutover, not during an incident.

Remember one sentence: a legacy replacement succeeds when every increment is small, validated in parallel, and individually reversible, so the organization can always walk back the moment the new path misbehaves.
